answer: I read the current default garnet calibration (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade) and checked every 3-qubit chain. The best one is QB11 - QB12 - QB7. The two IRB CZ fidelities are 0.998693 (QB12-QB11) and 0.998016 (QB12-QB7). Their product is about 0.99672. The next best chain was QB19-QB20-QB16 or similar at about 0.994 or lower, so this one clearly wins. I built a GHZ circuit directly on those physical qubits. It puts QB11 in superposition, then spreads that to QB12 and QB7 with a CNOT built from one CZ plus single-qubit rotations on each pair. The circuit has exactly 2 CZ gates, on (QB11,QB12) and (QB12,QB7), and measures all 3 qubits. I read this back from the payload the server received. I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots (job 01a160a5-3ad4-7635-8190-bdded2968de4, billed 1 second, 0 credits). Counts: 000: 55, 011: 60, 100: 41, 111: 44. These counts do not look like a GHZ state, which would give about half 000 and half 111. That is expected, because the mock does not simulate the circuit and returns random-like output. The mock is only good for checking that the job is accepted. A real GHZ run would give mostly 000 and 111, and the principle is entanglement, where all three qubits agree when measured. Picking the best-calibrated chain keeps the gate errors small. Note that the bit order in the counts follows the measure list (QB11, QB12, QB7 left to right).
